, a new approach has been developed that utilizes a hardware-assisted technique called Branch History Instrumentation (BHI). BHI leverages the capabilities of modern branch history information (BHI) hardware to identify and eliminate less frequent branching outcomes, thereby enhancing the performance of pipelined processors. The compiler generates small, hardware-based code segments that monitor branching history and feed this data back to the processor, allowing for optimized branch prediction. The compiler then uses this information to implement a technique called Branch Target Instrumentation (BTI), which reorders code to minimize the impact of less frequent branching outcomes. The compiler also inserts a branch to a small, dynamically allocated code region that handles rare branches, known as the branch history history region (HRR). The compiler optimizes the code by placing the HRR in a separate memory region, which can be accessed via branch target indirect jumps. The compiler also ensures that the HRR is not executed by implementing branch target protection instructions. The proposed BHI technique has been successfully implemented on a commercial processor, and experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness in boosting the performance of a variety of compiler-optimized programs.

the Cox proportional hazards model is a widely used tool for identifying key factors that influence the occurrence of an event. This method is then used to develop a test statistic that assesses the validity of the proportionality assumption. The proposed test is accompanied by an asymptotic distribution and a corresponding estimator for the time point at which proportionality is violated, if applicable. The method is further enhanced by a bootstrap-based approach to approximate the distribution of the test statistic, enabling the construction of a test with a known type I error rate. The proposed test is demonstrated to be effective in both simulated and real-world data analysis.
